name: Hermes
title: Messenger of the Gods and Guide of Souls
represents: Hermes rules the space between things: crossroads and boundaries, doorways, roads and the meeting of strangers. He is the herald of the gods, the patron of travellers, merchants, shepherds, athletes, orators and thieves, the god of lucky finds (a windfall was called a 'hermaion'), and the psychopomp who leads the souls of the dead down to Hades. He is quick, clever, charming and a little untrustworthy, a trickster who settles problems with wit and deals rather than force.
description:
The fullest early myth is the Homeric Hymn to Hermes (Hymn 4). Born at dawn in a cave on Mount Kyllene in Arcadia to the nymph Maia and Zeus, the infant Hermes had invented the lyre from a tortoise shell by noon, and that evening he stole fifty of Apollo's cattle, walking them backwards to hide their tracks. Brought before Zeus, he lied with such charm that the gods laughed. He made peace with Apollo by giving him the lyre, and Apollo in return gave him the herdsman's staff and authority over herds and certain kinds of divination. Homer's Odyssey shows him guiding the souls of the slain suitors to the underworld and giving Odysseus the herb moly to protect him against Circe's magic.

His worship was everywhere and down to earth. Herms, stone pillars topped with his head, stood at crossroads, boundaries and house doors, and travellers added stones to roadside cairns in his name. The fourth day of each month was his, and gymnasia held games called Hermaia. At the Anthesteria in Athens he was honoured as Chthonios, guide of the dead. The Romans identified him with Mercury, and in Hellenistic Egypt he merged with Thoth to become Hermes Trismegistus, the 'thrice-great' figure later credited with the Hermetic writings of alchemy and ceremonial magic.

Modern Hellenic polytheists (Hellenismos) honour Hermes with libations and hymns in the old style, while witches often turn to him for road opening, job hunts, exams, contracts, safe journeys and any message that needs to reach the right person. His link to Hermetic philosophy and to the planet Mercury comes from later astrology and Renaissance magic, layered on top of the ancient god.
items: herm pillar or roadside cairn stone
sacredDays: The fourth day of each lunar month; Wednesday (dies Mercurii) in Roman and later planetary tradition; the Hermaia athletic festivals; the third day of the Anthesteria (Chytroi) for Hermes Chthonios; any day you set out on a journey.
howToInvoke: Set a small altar near a door or threshold, or at a literal crossroads if it's safe. Light an orange or yellow candle and some light incense such as lavender or lemongrass, and put down a coin or a smooth stone as a 'herm'. Stand with your hands raised and palms up in the old Greek prayer posture, and call him by an epithet that fits what you need: Hodios for the road, Agoraios for business, Psychopompos for work with the dead. Pour a libation of wine, juice or water, and say plainly what message or opening you're asking for. He likes wit, so a joke, a riddle or a clever verse is welcome. Afterwards thank him, leave the coin for the next person to find or give it to someone who needs it, and keep your side of any bargain.
invocation:
Hermes of the crossroads, quick and bright,
Kyllene-born, you stole by night;
Herald with the serpent staff,
Who taught the gods themselves to laugh,
Open the road and clear the way,
Carry my words where they need to stay.
Guide of travellers, friend of the lost,
I pour this cup and count the cost.
Swift-foot Hermes, hear my call:
Luck at the gate and luck for all.
offerings: coins left at a crossroads or given away
a libation of wine, honey water or grape juice
honey cakes or sweet pastries
milk
a smooth stone added to a cairn or set on the altar
frankincense or lavender incense
a clever poem, riddle or well-told story
giving a stranger directions or a ride (an act of service)
a dice game played in his honour
avoid: Don't make him promises you won't keep, because he notices. Don't steal 'for' him; he protected thieves in myth, but the modern devotee honours his cleverness, not real harm to others. Keep offerings quick and tidy rather than leaving them to rot.
bestTime: Year-round; especially at the start of journeys, new jobs or exams, and during Mercury's direct motion (many witches avoid starting new contracts in Mercury retrograde, a modern astrological custom).
caution: Hermes is honoured in a living Hellenic polytheist tradition. He is a trickster, so be precise about what you ask for and don't treat him as a vending machine. Build a relationship over time and keep your word.

name: Selene
title: The Shining Moon Who Drives the Silver Chariot
represents: Selene is the Moon herself: the visible, shining disc crossing the night sky, not just a goddess who rules it. She marks the months, governs the night's light, inspires love and longing, and watches over sleepers and dreamers. She is gentle, radiant and wistful, the goddess of moonlit beauty and of the slow rhythms of waxing and waning.
description:
In Hesiod's Theogony Selene is a Titaness, daughter of Hyperion and Theia and sister of Helios (Sun) and Eos (Dawn). The short Homeric Hymn 32 praises her 'long-winged' radiance: she bathes in the ocean, puts on gleaming robes and yokes her shining horses in the evening, at the middle of the month when her orb is full. Her best-known myth is her love for the beautiful shepherd Endymion, who was granted endless sleep (by Zeus, or at her request) so that she could visit him every night on Mount Latmos, a story retold by poets from Sappho's time to Keats. Virgil (Georgics 3) has Pan win her with a gift of snow-white fleece.

Selene had little formal temple cult compared with the Olympians. She was honoured through the lunar calendar, at the new moon (noumenia) and full moon, and through folk magic. Greek love magic and the Greek Magical Papyri (Roman Egypt) are full of invocations to Selene, often merged with Hekate and Artemis as a threefold moon power, used for love, dreams and binding. Thessalian witches were said to be able to 'draw down the moon'.

Modern witches often honour Selene at the full moon, with moon water, silver candles and dreamwork. The phrase 'Drawing Down the Moon', central to Wiccan ritual, echoes those old Thessalian tales, but the modern rite is a twentieth-century creation, not a revival of a documented ancient ceremony.
items: mirror or bowl of water reflecting the moon
sacredDays: The full moon above all; the noumenia (first sliver of the new moon); Monday (Moon's day) in later tradition; clear nights through the year, especially autumn's harvest moon.
howToInvoke: Wait for a clear night near the full moon. Set a bowl of water where it catches her light, place a white or silver candle and a moonstone or selenite beside it, and stand barefoot facing her. Raise both hands toward the Moon and greet her by name. Speak softly; this is a goddess of gentle radiance, not thunder. Ask for clear dreams, soothing, beauty or the gradual growth of something you love. Let the bowl sit in the moonlight as you sing or recite the invocation. Afterwards thank her, pour some of the moon water onto the earth or a plant, and keep the rest for dream and beauty work.
invocation:
Selene, silver-crowned and bright,
Driver of the steeds of night,
Bathe my bowl in your soft fire,
Fill my sleep with sweet desire.
As you wax, let my hopes grow;
As you wane, let my sorrows go.
Lady who loved the sleeping one,
Watch me dream till night is done.
offerings: moon water poured back to the earth
white flowers such as jasmine or white roses
round honey cakes or crescent-shaped cookies
milk or honeyed milk
a white or silver candle
a love poem read aloud by moonlight
a dream journal kept in her honour
a song or soft music played outside at night
avoid: Avoid harsh banishing or cursing in her name; she is not a goddess of vengeance. Don't leave candles burning unattended overnight while you sleep.
bestTime: Clear nights all year; especially the Full Moon and the autumn Harvest and Hunter's Moons (Sep–Oct).
caution: Many modern sources mix Selene, Artemis, Hekate and Diana into one 'moon goddess'. That merging has real roots in late antique magic, but each goddess has her own history, so honour Selene as herself.

name: Pan
title: Goat-Footed Lord of the Wild
represents: Pan is the untamed countryside: mountain pasture, pine forest, goat flocks, the hot hush of noon and the sudden terror that grips a lonely traveller or an army ('panic'). He is the god of shepherds and herds, rustic music, hunting luck, wild sexuality and the vitality of nature in its raw, uncultivated form: playful, earthy, lusty and unpredictable.
description:
Pan began as a local god of Arcadia, the rugged mountain heart of the Peloponnese. The Homeric Hymn to Pan (Hymn 19) calls him the son of Hermes and a daughter of Dryops, born goat-footed, horned and bearded, so that his nurse fled in fright, but the gods all delighted in him. In Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book 1) he pursues the nymph Syrinx, who is turned into marsh reeds; from those reeds he made the panpipes. Other stories tell of the nymphs Pitys (turned into a pine) and Echo.

Herodotus (6.105) reports that before the Battle of Marathon the runner Pheidippides met Pan on the road, and the Athenians afterwards founded a cult to him in a cave below the Acropolis. Cave shrines to Pan and the nymphs, with rustic offerings and votive reliefs, are found across Greece. Plutarch (On the Obsolescence of Oracles) tells the eerie story of a sailor hearing a voice cry 'Great Pan is dead!', which later Christians read as the end of the pagan age.

Pan was reborn in Romantic and Edwardian literature as the spirit of nature, from Kenneth Grahame's 'The Piper at the Gates of Dawn' to Aleister Crowley's 'Hymn to Pan', and he strongly shaped the Wiccan image of the Horned God. Modern pagans honour him as a joyful, wild nature god; Hellenic polytheists honour him in his older Arcadian form. The horned 'Pan' of modern witchcraft is partly a modern composite figure.
sacredDays: Noon (the old 'hour of Pan', when shepherds feared to disturb his rest); Beltane and the height of summer in modern paganism; spring lambing season.
howToInvoke: Go outdoors if you can, into woods, meadow or hillside, or set a green candle beside a pine cone, a sprig of greenery and a cup of wine or juice. Play music, even just a whistle, a drum or a reed flute, or put on wild pipe music. Invoke him with laughter and energy rather than solemnity: dance, stamp your feet, breathe the open air. Ask for vitality, a return of joy, creative wildness, or a blessing on your garden or animals. Leave the place cleaner than you found it as your thanks, and close by pouring the drink onto the earth.
invocation:
Io Pan! Goat-foot, horned and free,
Piper beneath the greenwood tree,
Lord of the hill and the shepherd's fold,
Wild as the mountain, warm as gold.
Wake the blood and stir the root,
Bless the blossom and the fruit.
Play your reeds and I will dance:
Io Pan, Pan, Pan!
offerings: wine, mead or honey water poured onto the ground
goat's-milk cheese or milk
honey and honeycomb
fresh fruit, nuts and figs
a pine cone or pine garland
music played outdoors, especially pipes or flute
dancing and laughter in his honour
picking up litter in a wild place
supporting a local farm or sanctuary for goats and sheep
avoid: Don't disturb him at noon, according to the old shepherd's taboo. Don't approach him with grim, stiff formality. Never use his myths to excuse sexual coercion; modern devotees honour his vitality and joy, and consent is non-negotiable.
bestTime: Late spring and summer, Beltane to Midsummer (May–June), and lambing season.
caution: Several of Pan's myths involve pursuing unwilling nymphs. Read them as ancient stories, not models of behaviour. His energy can be overwhelming ('panic'), so ground yourself afterwards.

name: Diana
altNames: Queen of the Witches (Italian folk tradition)
title: Lady of the Sacred Grove and Queen of the Witches
represents: Diana is the Roman goddess of wild woodland and the hunt, of the moon, and of women, especially in childbirth. She protects the vulnerable, the free and the untamed, and was honoured by both slaves and nobles. Over the centuries she also became the 'goddess of the witches' in European folklore, the queen of a night-riding host and the divine mother at the heart of several modern witchcraft traditions.
description:
Diana was an ancient Italic goddess before the Romans identified her with the Greek Artemis. Her most famous sanctuary stood in a sacred grove by Lake Nemi near Aricia, where she was Diana Nemorensis, 'of the grove'. Her priest there, the rex Nemorensis, was traditionally a runaway slave who won the office by killing his predecessor after breaking a bough from a sacred tree, a custom James Frazer made the starting point of The Golden Bough. Her temple on Rome's Aventine Hill, said to be founded by King Servius Tullius, celebrated its dedication on the Ides of August (13 August), a holiday for slaves.

On that date women walked to Nemi carrying torches, the whole lake glittering with their lights, to give thanks for prayers answered; poets such as Ovid (Fasti) and Statius (Silvae 3.1) describe the scene, with hunting dogs garlanded and rested for the day. Votive offerings found at Nemi include terracotta models of body parts and of mothers and babies, evidence of prayers for healing and safe childbirth. She was also Diana Triformis, linked with Luna and Hecate as a threefold goddess of crossroads and night.

In medieval Europe, the tenth-century Canon Episcopi condemned women who believed they rode out at night 'with Diana, goddess of the pagans', a belief that fed later witch-lore. Charles Leland's 'Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches' (1899) claimed to record Tuscan witches who worshipped Diana and her daughter Aradia; its authenticity is debated, but it deeply shaped Wicca. Today Diana is honoured in Roman revivalist practice (Religio Romana), in Stregheria, and in Dianic Wicca, a women-centred tradition founded in the 1970s. Many witches now celebrate the Nemoralia on 13 August with candles reflected in water.
sacredDays: The Nemoralia (Ides of August, 13 August, and in modern practice often 13–15 August); the full moon; Monday; childbirth and coming-of-age rites.
howToInvoke: Bathe or wash your hair beforehand (Roman women washed and adorned their hair for the festival). Set up your altar outside under trees if you can, or beside a bowl of water to stand in for Lake Nemi. Light a white candle (or several) so the flames reflect in the water, and place a moonstone, a sprig of greenery and a ribbon or a written prayer there. Stand tall, raise your hands, and speak to her as protector and huntress. Ask for courage, independence, protection for yourself or for women and children in your life, or healing. Leave a written prayer or ribbon as a votive, a modern stand-in for the ancient clay offerings. Afterwards give thanks, put out the flames safely, and do something generous for an animal or a woman in need.
invocation:
Diana of the moonlit grove,
Huntress, keeper, queen of the night,
Your torches dance on Nemi's glass,
Your silver bow draws pure and bright.
Guard the wild and guard the free,
Guard the mother and the child,
Lend me courage, keen and clear,
Lady of the green and wild.
Three-formed goddess, hear my plea:
As I will, so let it be.
offerings: white candles or small lanterns floated or reflected in water
a ribbon or written prayer tied to a tree
fresh water from a spring or stream
apples, pears or grapes
small cakes or bread
white or wild flowers
garlands placed on a dog's collar and a day of rest for your hounds
donations to wildlife rescue or women's shelters
a walk through the woods in silence
avoid: Don't cut living trees from a grove for her rituals; take fallen wood. Avoid hunting trophies or other animal parts as offerings. Respect her protection of the vulnerable: don't use her name for spells of control over another person.
bestTime: Late summer, especially the Nemoralia (13 August), and moonlit nights year-round.
caution: Leland's Aradia and later Diana-centred witchcraft are modern or folk-modern sources, not ancient Roman scripture. Dianic Wicca is one tradition among many with its own boundaries. Always practise fire safety with candles near water and trees.

name: Isis
title: Great of Magic, Mother of Horus
represents: Isis is the great magician of the Egyptian gods, the faithful wife who gathered and restored her murdered husband Osiris, the protective mother who hid and healed the infant Horus, and the divine throne itself (her name is written with the hieroglyph of a seat). She embodies devoted love, mourning that leads to rebirth, the power of words and secret names, healing of the sick and protection of children. In the Greco-Roman world she grew into a universal goddess of the cosmos, the seas and salvation.
description:
Isis appears in the Pyramid Texts of the Old Kingdom (c. 2400 BCE), where she and her sister Nephthys mourn and protect the dead king, identified with Osiris. The fullest connected telling of the Osiris myth is Greek: Plutarch's On Isis and Osiris (1st–2nd century CE) tells how Set murdered Osiris and scattered his body, how Isis searched the land in grief, found and gathered the pieces, and through her magic conceived Horus. Egyptian texts add the story of her raising Horus in the papyrus marshes of Khemmis and healing him from scorpion stings, and a New Kingdom tale in which she tricks the aging sun god Ra into revealing his secret name, gaining supreme magical power.

Her cult grew over time, centred on temples such as Philae near Aswan, one of the last Egyptian temples to function, closed under Emperor Justinian in the 6th century CE. The knot-shaped tyet amulet, often carved from red stone such as carnelian or red jasper, was called the 'blood of Isis'. Spreading across the Mediterranean, Isis became the focus of mystery initiations: Apuleius' novel The Golden Ass (Book 11) describes her appearing from the sea crowned with the moon, and the spring Navigium Isidis festival launched a ship in her honour to open the sailing season.

Today Isis is honoured by Kemetic revivalists, who call her Aset and follow temple-based practice, and in many forms of Western esotericism, goddess spirituality and witchcraft, where she is invoked as the great mother, healer and mistress of magic. Some Western images of her (such as the 'veiled Isis' of Romantic esotericism) are later inventions, not Egyptian. Egyptian religion is honoured today as a living path by Kemetic revivalists, including Kemetic Orthodoxy and many independent reconstructionists, who draw carefully on temple texts and scholarship. Approach with humility, learn some history of ancient Egypt, and don't treat Egyptian imagery as mere decoration.
items: horns and sun disk crown (borrowed from Hathor)
planet: Moon (Greco-Roman association); the star Sirius (Sopdet), whose rising heralded the Nile flood
sacredDays: The heliacal rising of Sirius and the Nile inundation season (July–August); the Navigium Isidis (5 March) in the Roman world; the Isia and the festival of the 'finding of Osiris' (late October–early November); the epagomenal (extra) days of the Egyptian year, the fourth of which was her birthday.
howToInvoke: Purify yourself first: wash your hands and face and rinse your mouth, as Egyptian priests purified before entering the temple. Set up a clean altar with a white cloth, a vessel of fresh water, a white or blue candle, and her image or symbol (a throne, wings or tyet knot). Light myrrh or frankincense. Stand with arms raised or kneel with palms up, and greet her with praise before asking anything; Egyptian prayers open with praise and titles. Ask for healing, protection for a child or loved one, comfort in grief, or the strength to rebuild what was broken. Make your offering, sit quietly in her presence, then thank her. In Kemetic custom, food offerings are later 'reverted' (shared by the worshipper) or respectfully disposed of rather than left to spoil.
invocation:
Aset, Great of Magic, Lady of the Throne,
You who searched the river reeds alone,
Who gathered what was broken and made it whole,
Who breathed with your wings new life into the soul,
Spread those wings above me now,
Your sun-disk shining on your brow.
Mother of Horus, mistress of the Name,
Heal what is wounded, guard what is mine;
I come in praise and lift my hands,
Queen of the stars and the black land's sands.
offerings: fresh, cool water
bread or small cakes
beer or wine (or grape juice)
milk
blue lotus flowers, roses or other fresh flowers
myrrh, frankincense or kyphi-style incense
perfumed oil
hymns or praise poetry recited aloud
care for children, the sick or the grieving in her name
donations to medical or maternal-health charities
avoid: Approach with ritual cleanliness. In Kemetic practice, avoid bringing obvious impurity (e.g. unwashed hands) before her shrine. Don't use her imagery purely as fashion or decoration. Treat her as a real goddess, not a 'goddess archetype' to be used.
bestTime: High summer, the rising of Sirius and the Nile flood season (Jul–Aug); also late October–early November for the mysteries of mourning and rebirth.
caution: Egyptian religion is honoured today as a living path by Kemetic revivalists, including Kemetic Orthodoxy and many independent reconstructionists, who draw carefully on temple texts and scholarship. Approach with humility, learn some history of ancient Egypt, and don't treat Egyptian imagery as mere decoration. Much popular 'Isis' lore mixes Egyptian, Greco-Roman and Victorian esoteric material, so check your sources.

name: Bastet
title: Lady of Bubastis, the Fierce and Gentle Cat
represents: Bastet is the protective goddess of home and hearth, of women, children and childbirth, of joy, music, dance and perfume. She protects against disease and evil spirits. As an 'Eye of Ra' she is the sun god's fierce daughter, first imagined as a lioness and later mainly as a cat or cat-headed woman. She holds two sides in balance: the tender, purring guardian of the household and the claws that defend it.
description:
Bastet was worshipped from at least the Second Dynasty (c. 2800 BCE), when she was shown as a lioness, close in nature to Sekhmet. Her cult centre was Bubastis (Per-Bast, today's Tell Basta) in the Nile Delta. Her importance peaked in the Third Intermediate and Late Periods, when Bubastite kings ruled Egypt and the gentler cat form became dominant. The Pyramid Texts call her a protector of the king, and later texts make her a daughter of Ra and an Eye of Ra who fights the sun's enemies.

The Greek historian Herodotus (Histories 2.59–60, 137–138) visited Bubastis in the 5th century BCE and described its beautiful temple, set on an island between canals and shaded by trees, and its festival: hundreds of thousands of pilgrims sailing in boats, with music, clapping, singing, dancing and more wine drunk than all the rest of the year. Huge cat cemeteries were found at Bubastis and elsewhere. Note that many of those cats were bred to be mummified as votive offerings, which is a sobering part of the historical record.

Greeks equated her with Artemis, which led to later lunar associations, though in Egyptian thought she was mainly solar. Her link to perfume (the ointment jar was called 'bas') appears in some texts, though the exact origin of her name is uncertain. Today Bastet is honoured by Kemetic revivalists and is a popular goddess among modern witches and cat lovers, called on for home protection, joy, sensuality and the welfare of cats. Egyptian religion is honoured today as a living path by Kemetic revivalists, including Kemetic Orthodoxy and many independent reconstructionists, who draw carefully on temple texts and scholarship. Approach with humility, learn some history of ancient Egypt, and don't treat Egyptian imagery as mere decoration.
items: aegis (broad collar with a lioness head)
sacredDays: Her great festival at Bubastis, celebrated in spring according to some calendars; many modern devotees mark Bastet on their own chosen festival days (e.g. 31 October in some modern lists, a modern custom). Sunny days and any time you welcome a new cat into the home are also hers.
howToInvoke: Clean your home first; she is a goddess of the well-kept household. Set up a small altar with a cat figurine or image, a gold or green candle, a dish of fresh water and a few drops of perfume or perfumed oil. Shake a rattle or play music, since joy and noise were part of her worship. Speak her name and titles, and ask for protection for your home, children and pets, for a return of joy and playfulness, or for help with a pregnancy or creative project. Spend time with your cats or with animals in need as part of the rite. Thank her, and in Kemetic custom share the food offering afterwards rather than wasting it.
invocation:
Bastet, Lady of Bubastis' shore,
Golden-eyed guardian at my door,
Sistrum shaking, perfume sweet,
Soft as velvet, swift of feet.
Purr upon my hearth and home,
Guard my kin where'er they roam,
Claws for the foe and love for the kind,
Joy in my heart and peace in my mind.
offerings: perfume or perfumed oil (a drop on the altar)
fresh, cool water
music, rattling, dancing and singing
beer or wine (or juice) in a small cup
bread or sweet cakes
a candle in gold or green
donations or volunteering at a cat rescue or animal shelter
taking excellent care of your own cats (vet visits, play, attention)
flowers such as blue lotus or jasmine
avoid: Never harm, neglect or 'sacrifice' a cat; do not use animal parts. Keep essential oils, lilies and incense smoke away from real cats: many oils and lilies are toxic to them. Offer catnip to living cats, not burned.
bestTime: Spring and high summer, under bright sun; or any time you bless a home or welcome a new pet.
caution: Egyptian religion is honoured today as a living path by Kemetic revivalists, including Kemetic Orthodoxy and many independent reconstructionists, who draw carefully on temple texts and scholarship. Approach with humility, learn some history of ancient Egypt, and don't treat Egyptian imagery as mere decoration. Bastet's popularity in modern 'cat goddess' culture has created much invented lore, so prefer sources that cite Egyptian evidence. Keep cats away from candles, oils and incense.

name: Thoth
title: Lord of Divine Words, Scribe of the Gods
represents: Thoth is the god of writing, hieroglyphs, language and knowledge; the scribe and record-keeper of the gods; the reckoner of time, mathematics and the lunar calendar; and a patron of magic, medicine and law. He mediates disputes, records the verdict at the judgement of the dead, and heals the injured Eye of Horus. He is calm, exact and endlessly learned, the divine mind that brings order through words.
description:
Thoth, Egyptian Djehuty, was depicted as an ibis-headed man or as a baboon, the animal thought to greet the dawn. His cult centre was Khemenu (Greek Hermopolis) in Middle Egypt, home of a creation myth of eight primeval deities (the Ogdoad). He appears throughout Egyptian religious literature: in the Pyramid Texts he helps the king cross the sky, and in Book of the Dead Spell 125 he records the result when the heart of the deceased is weighed against the feather of Ma'at. Myth credits him with healing Horus' eye after his fight with Set, and with judging between Horus and Set.

Plutarch (On Isis and Osiris) relates that Thoth won five extra days from the Moon at a board game, creating the epagomenal days on which Osiris, Isis, Set, Nephthys and Horus the Elder were born. The first month of the Egyptian calendar bore his name. Egyptian scribes poured a few drops of water from their ink palettes in his honour before writing, and countless ibis and baboon mummies were dedicated at his sanctuaries. Demotic stories such as the tale of Setne Khamwas tell of a dangerous 'Book of Thoth' containing spells that gave power over heaven and earth.

In Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt, Greeks identified Thoth with Hermes, producing Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetica and patron of Western alchemy, astrology and ceremonial magic. Modern occult works such as the 'Emerald Tablets of Thoth' (a 20th-century text by Doreal) are not ancient Egyptian. Today Thoth (Djehuty) is honoured in Kemetic practice and by students, writers and magicians who seek his wisdom. Egyptian religion is honoured today as a living path by Kemetic revivalists, including Kemetic Orthodoxy and many independent reconstructionists, who draw carefully on temple texts and scholarship. Approach with humility, learn some history of ancient Egypt, and don't treat Egyptian imagery as mere decoration.
sacredDays: Wepet Renpet (Egyptian New Year, tied to the rising of Sirius) and the month of Djehuty that opened the year; the festival of Thoth (Djehutyet) around day 19 of that month; the new moon; Wednesday in later Hermetic tradition.
howToInvoke: Clean and order your workspace; Thoth loves exactness. Set a white or deep-blue candle beside a notebook, pen and a small cup of clean water, and burn frankincense. Before you begin, pour a few drops of water in his honour, as ancient scribes did. Address him with titles such as Lord of Divine Words or Lord of the Moon and ask for clear thought, memory, eloquence, help with study or writing, or fair judgement in a dispute. Then do the work: write, study or carefully record your thoughts as an offering. Close by thanking him and writing the date and what you learned.
invocation:
Djehuty, Lord of Divine Words,
Ibis wise and silver-crowned,
Keeper of the reckoning moon,
In whose ink all truth is bound,
Steady my hand, make clear my sight,
Let my words be wise and right.
Scribe who weighs the heart with care,
Teach me as I study there.
I pour this water from my pen:
Write wisdom in my heart again.
offerings: drops of clean water poured from an ink pot or pen
fresh ink, quality paper or a new notebook
a page of your own careful writing or translation
frankincense or myrrh incense
bread or figs
honest study or a lesson completed in his name
teaching someone else a skill
donations to libraries, literacy programs or ibis conservation
beer or wine (or juice)
avoid: Avoid lies, plagiarism, broken contracts and careless sloppiness in his name. Don't present the 20th-century 'Emerald Tablets of Thoth' as ancient Egyptian. Don't make his altar cluttered or dirty.
bestTime: The Egyptian New Year season (late July–August); also autumn study season and the start of any course or writing project.
caution: Egyptian religion is honoured today as a living path by Kemetic revivalists, including Kemetic Orthodoxy and many independent reconstructionists, who draw carefully on temple texts and scholarship. Approach with humility, learn some history of ancient Egypt, and don't treat Egyptian imagery as mere decoration. Much modern 'Thoth' material is New Age invention, so tell ancient Egyptian evidence apart from later Hermetic and 20th-century lore.

name: Anubis
altNames: Tepy-dju-ef (He Who Is upon His Mountain)
title: Guardian of the Necropolis, Opener of the Ways
represents: Anubis is the god of mummification and embalming, guardian of cemeteries and tombs, and guide and protector of the dead on their journey to the afterlife. He tends the scales at the Weighing of the Heart, watches over the burial and the body, and prepares the dead for rebirth. His black colour stands for the fertile Nile silt and for the rebirth promised to the dead, as well as for the dark of the tomb. Watchful, protective and faithful, he walks beside those in transition.
description:
Anubis is one of Egypt's oldest gods. His jackal or canine image (probably based on the African golden wolf that haunted desert-edge cemeteries) appears from the Early Dynastic period, and he dominates Old Kingdom funerary prayers before Osiris rose to prominence. In the myth told later, he embalmed the murdered Osiris, creating the first mummy, which is why embalming priests wore jackal masks while they worked. His fetish, the imiut, was a headless animal skin hung on a pole, and he was worshipped especially at Cynopolis ('Dog City') and at cemeteries throughout Egypt.

In the Book of the Dead, especially the vignettes of Spell 125, Anubis leads the deceased into the Hall of Two Truths and adjusts the scales on which the heart is weighed against the feather of Ma'at, while Thoth records the result. As Wepwawet's close companion and an 'opener of the ways', he guarded the paths of the dead. In Greco-Roman times he merged with Hermes as Hermanubis, a psychopomp, and his cult travelled with Isis around the Mediterranean.

Modern Kemetic practitioners honour Anubis as a protector of the dead and of the living in transition. Modern witches and death workers often call on him in ancestor veneration, grief work, hospice and end-of-life care, and for protection. Egyptian religion is honoured today as a living path by Kemetic revivalists, including Kemetic Orthodoxy and many independent reconstructionists, who draw carefully on temple texts and scholarship. Approach with humility, learn some history of ancient Egypt, and don't treat Egyptian imagery as mere decoration.
planet: Pluto (modern correspondence; no ancient planetary link)
sacredDays: Funerals and memorials; the Egyptian 'Beautiful Festival of the Valley' honouring the dead; the anniversaries of loved ones' deaths; in modern practice, Samhain and Day of the Dead seasons (late October–early November).
howToInvoke: Set up a dark-cloth altar with a black or white candle, a black jackal or dog image, a cup of water, bread, and myrrh or frankincense. If you're honouring a specific ancestor, add their photo or name. Purify yourself by washing hands and face. Stand or kneel, greet Anubis with his titles, and ask him to protect and guide your beloved dead, to help you through grief, or to guard your home and path at night. Speak the names of your dead. Sit in silence for a while, then thank him, put out the candle, and share or respectfully dispose of the food. Doing a kindness for a dog, or tending a grave, makes a good closing act.
invocation:
Anpu, Lord of the Sacred Land,
Watcher with the steady hand,
Black as the silt where new life grows,
Keeper of what the west wind knows,
Guard the ones who walked before,
Guide them gently through the door.
Opener of the hidden way,
Walk with me through night and day.
Weigh my heart and find it true;
I offer bread and water to you.
offerings: fresh water and bread
myrrh, frankincense or cedar incense
a black or white candle
speaking the names of your dead
tending graves or cleaning a neglected cemetery
volunteering at a dog shelter or hospice
linen or a clean white cloth
beer or wine (or juice) in a small cup
dates or figs
avoid: Never desecrate graves or take bones, earth or objects from cemeteries without permission. Don't harm or neglect dogs. Avoid treating him only as a 'spooky' aesthetic; he is gentle with the dead and serious about his duties.
bestTime: Autumn into early winter, especially late October–November; also during mourning, at funerals and on death anniversaries.
caution: Egyptian religion is honoured today as a living path by Kemetic revivalists, including Kemetic Orthodoxy and many independent reconstructionists, who draw carefully on temple texts and scholarship. Approach with humility, learn some history of ancient Egypt, and don't treat Egyptian imagery as mere decoration. Death and grief work can be emotionally heavy; seek human support too and never use spirit work in place of professional help for grief or crisis.

name: Freyja
title: Lady of the Vanir, Mistress of Seiðr
represents: Freyja is the radiant Vanir goddess of love, desire, beauty and fertility, of gold and wealth, and also of war and death, since she chooses half the battle-slain for her hall. She is the mistress of seiðr, a Norse form of trance magic and prophecy, which she taught to the Æsir. Proud, passionate and independent, she weeps tears of red gold for her wandering husband and travels in a chariot drawn by cats or on her golden-bristled boar.
description:
Freyja is known mainly from Old Icelandic sources of the 13th century: the Poetic Edda and Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda and Ynglinga saga. She is the daughter of the sea god Njörðr and sister of Freyr, one of the Vanir who came to live among the Æsir after the war between the two divine families. In Grímnismál (st. 14) she chooses half the slain each day for her field Fólkvangr, while Odin takes the other half. Snorri's Gylfaginning says her hall is Sessrúmnir, that she rides in a cart pulled by two cats, and that she wept red gold searching for her husband Óðr. Ynglinga saga (ch. 4) says she first taught seiðr to the Æsir.

She owns the famous necklace Brísingamen, which in Þrymskviða bursts when she is furious at being demanded as a giant's bride, and a falcon-feather cloak that lets the wearer fly. In Hyndluljóð she rides the boar Hildisvíni. Place-names across Scandinavia and the Viking-age practice of seiðr, performed by seeresses (völur) such as the one described in Eiríks saga rauða, hint at her real cult, though how she was worshipped before Christianisation is uncertain and much of our picture comes through Christian-era writers.

Today Freyja is one of the most beloved goddesses in Heathenry and in the wider pagan world. Heathens honour her in blót (offering rites) and sumbel (ritual toasting), and many seiðr and spæ (prophecy) workers see her as their patron. Modern witches invoke her for self-love, sensuality, abundance, magical power and courage. Associations with specific herbs and stones are mostly modern. Norse gods are worshipped today in Heathenry (Ásatrú, Forn Sed and related paths), a living religion with its own customs. Mainstream Heathen organisations reject racism and 'folkish' gatekeeping: no one is barred from the gods by ancestry. Steer clear of symbols and slogans taken up by hate groups (such as the 'Black Sun', the winged Othala rune, or white-power slogans dressed up as Norse lore), and check where your Norse imagery comes from.
animals: ladybird (called 'Freyja's hen' in some Scandinavian folk names)
sacredDays: Friday (in many modern practices, though the name may come from Frigg); Dísablót and Winter Nights (Vetrnætr) in late autumn; spring and May festivals in modern practice; Valentine's season for love work in modern devotion.
howToInvoke: Set an altar with a gold or green candle, amber or gold jewellery, fresh flowers and a horn or glass of mead. Dress up a little; she delights in beauty and confidence. Hail her by name ('Hail Freyja!') with your arms raised, then speak to her plainly and with self-respect. She doesn't like grovelling. Ask for love, self-worth, abundance, courage, or guidance in seiðr and prophecy. Raise the horn, speak a toast or vow, drink a sip and pour the rest as her share (outside onto the earth, or into an offering bowl to pour out later). Close with thanks, and honour her by acting with confidence and generosity.
invocation:
Hail Freyja, Lady of the Vanir bright,
Gold-tear weeper, falcon of flight,
Brísingamen gleams upon your breast,
Sessrúmnir's queen, of all the best.
Teach me seiðr, open my sight,
Kindle my love and my own delight,
Lady of battle and lady of bed,
Crown me with courage, gold and red.
Hail Freyja!
offerings: mead or honey wine (or sparkling apple juice)
honey and honey cakes
fresh flowers, especially roses
strawberries or other sweet fruit
amber or gold jewellery dedicated to her
chocolate or fine sweets (a modern favourite)
a heartfelt love poem or song
dancing or making yourself beautiful in her honour
caring for cats or donating to animal rescues
a toast made in sumbel
avoid: Don't approach her with shame about your body or desire, or try to bind someone's love against their will in her name. Avoid symbols co-opted by hate groups. Don't break oaths made over a horn to her.
bestTime: Spring through midsummer for love and fertility (Apr–Jun), and late autumn's Winter Nights and Dísablót (Oct–Nov) for seiðr and the dísir.
caution: Norse gods are worshipped today in Heathenry (Ásatrú, Forn Sed and related paths), a living religion with its own customs. Mainstream Heathen organisations reject racism and 'folkish' gatekeeping: no one is barred from the gods by ancestry. Steer clear of symbols and slogans taken up by hate groups (such as the 'Black Sun', the winged Othala rune, or white-power slogans dressed up as Norse lore), and check where your Norse imagery comes from. Seiðr and trance work should be learned carefully and grounded afterwards.

name: Odin
title: Allfather, Wanderer, Winner of the Runes
represents: Odin is the restless seeker of wisdom: god of poetry and ecstatic inspiration, runes and magic, war and the honoured dead, kingship and cunning, and the wanderer who travels the worlds in disguise. He sacrificed himself to himself to win the runes, gave an eye for a drink from Mímir's well, and stole the mead of poetry. He is a complex, challenging, often unpredictable god, generous with insight and demanding of courage.
description:
Wodanaz, the Germanic ancestor of Odin, is attested by the Roman era (Tacitus identified a chief god of the Germans with Mercury), and his name lives on in English 'Wednesday'. Our richest sources are Old Norse: the Poetic Edda and Snorri's Prose Edda (13th century). In Hávamál (st. 138–141) Odin says he hung on a wind-swept tree for nine nights, wounded by a spear, 'given to Odin, myself to myself', until he looked down, took up the runes, and fell back screaming. Gylfaginning and Völuspá tell of his eye pledged at Mímir's well, his ravens Huginn ('thought') and Muninn ('memory'), his eight-legged horse Sleipnir, his spear Gungnir, the ring Draupnir, and his hall Valhalla, where chosen warriors await Ragnarök.

Skáldskaparmál tells how he won the mead of poetry from the giant Suttungr through seduction and shape-shifting, which is why poets called verse 'Odin's mead'. Viking-age kings and warriors sought his favour, and Old English charms such as the Nine Herbs Charm show Woden as a healer who struck a serpent with nine 'glory-twigs'. In later folklore across Scandinavia and Germany he leads the Wild Hunt on stormy winter nights, and one of his names, Jólnir, ties him to Yule.

In modern Heathenry, Odin is honoured in blót and sumbel with mead, poetry and oaths, and many people turn to him for rune-work, study, creativity and courage in hard times. He's a popular figure in pop culture, but devotees find him far more complex than his film version. Norse gods are worshipped today in Heathenry (Ásatrú, Forn Sed and related paths), a living religion with its own customs. Mainstream Heathen organisations reject racism and 'folkish' gatekeeping: no one is barred from the gods by ancestry. Steer clear of symbols and slogans taken up by hate groups (such as the 'Black Sun', the winged Othala rune, or white-power slogans dressed up as Norse lore), and check where your Norse imagery comes from.
sacredDays: Wednesday (Wōden's day); Yule and the Twelve Nights (Wild Hunt season); Winter Nights; storm-filled nights; any time you take up the runes or make a solemn vow.
howToInvoke: Odin is best approached at a sumbel or blót, or quietly with a single candle, a horn or cup of mead, and runes or a notebook on the altar. Hail him by name ('Hail Odin, Allfather!') and speak with honesty and boldness, because he values courage and wit over flattery. A poem, even an imperfect one, is a classic gift. Ask for wisdom, inspiration, insight through runes, or strength to face a difficult truth; be ready for the answer to come as a challenge. Toast, drink, and pour his share. Close with thanks. Many Heathens advise against swearing big oaths to him lightly.
invocation:
Hail, Allfather, Wanderer grey,
Who hung nine nights on the windswept tree,
Who gave an eye at Mímir's well,
And won the runes that set words free,
Raven-god of thought and memory,
Bright mead-giver of the skald,
Grant me wisdom, hard and true,
And courage when the dark has called.
Hail Odin!
offerings: mead (or a fine dark beer, whisky, or non-alcoholic alternative)
an original poem or story recited aloud
bread and a portion of a shared meal
carving or painting a rune with care
dedicated study of history, language or poetry
tobacco-free incense of juniper or mugwort
keeping your word and making honest oaths
a gift of hospitality to a traveller or stranger (he travels in disguise)
feeding birds such as crows and ravens where permitted
avoid: Don't break oaths, especially those sworn on a horn or ring. Avoid racialised 'folkish' interpretations and symbols co-opted by hate groups. Don't seek him only for battle-fury or domination; he is also a god of hospitality, wisdom and poetry.
bestTime: Autumn through Yule, especially the dark, stormy nights of Winter Nights to the Twelve Nights of Yule (Oct–Jan).
caution: Norse gods are worshipped today in Heathenry (Ásatrú, Forn Sed and related paths), a living religion with its own customs. Mainstream Heathen organisations reject racism and 'folkish' gatekeeping: no one is barred from the gods by ancestry. Steer clear of symbols and slogans taken up by hate groups (such as the 'Black Sun', the winged Othala rune, or white-power slogans dressed up as Norse lore), and check where your Norse imagery comes from. Odin is a powerful, often difficult god; devotees describe him as testing. Keep your word, ground yourself after rune or trance work, and don't treat him as a vending machine.

name: Frigg
title: Queen of Ásgarðr, Who Knows All Fates
represents: Frigg is the queen of the gods and wife of Odin, the goddess of marriage, motherhood, household management and hospitality, and of spinning, both of thread and of fate. She knows all destinies but does not speak them. She protects children and families, oversees the hearth and the keys of the household, and grieves deeply for her son Baldr. She is wise, dignified and quietly powerful, sharing Odin's high seat Hliðskjálf from which all worlds can be seen.
description:
Frigg (from Proto-Germanic Frijjō) was honoured widely across the Germanic world; the English 'Friday' most likely preserves her name. The 7th-century Lombard origin story (Origo Gentis Langobardorum) tells how Frea outwitted her husband Godan to grant victory and a name to her favoured people. The Second Merseburg Charm, a 10th-century Old High German healing charm, names Frija among the goddesses who sing over a horse's injured leg.

In Old Norse sources she lives in Fensalir ('fen halls'). In Lokasenna (st. 29), Freyja declares that Frigg knows all fates though she speaks them not. Snorri's Gylfaginning tells the most moving story: troubled by her son Baldr's dreams, Frigg took oaths from fire, water, metals, stones, plants, beasts and illnesses not to harm him, but overlooked the young mistletoe. Loki guided the blind god Höðr to throw a mistletoe dart, and Baldr died. Frigg then asked for someone to ride to Hel and bargain for his return. She is attended by handmaidens such as Fulla, keeper of her casket, Hlín the protector, and Gná the swift messenger.

In Swedish folk tradition the stars of Orion's Belt were sometimes called 'Frigg's distaff' (Friggerock). Modern Heathens honour Frigg as matron of the household and family, and often link her with Mother's Night (Mōdraniht, mentioned by Bede) at the start of Yule, a modern association drawn from an Anglo-Saxon festival whose exact deities are unknown. Witches call on her for home blessing, family protection, wise foresight, and the spinning of good fortune. Norse gods are worshipped today in Heathenry (Ásatrú, Forn Sed and related paths), a living religion with its own customs. Mainstream Heathen organisations reject racism and 'folkish' gatekeeping: no one is barred from the gods by ancestry. Steer clear of symbols and slogans taken up by hate groups (such as the 'Black Sun', the winged Othala rune, or white-power slogans dressed up as Norse lore), and check where your Norse imagery comes from.
planet: Venus (through Friday); some modern practitioners link her to the Moon
sacredDays: Friday; Mother's Night (the eve of Yule, around 20–21 December in modern practice); Yule season; weddings, births and house-warmings.
howToInvoke: Tidy the house first; even one clean, ordered corner is welcome. Set out a blue or white candle, a set of keys, some yarn or a spindle, and a cup of mead, tea or milk. Sit quietly, perhaps while spinning, knitting or doing some other handwork, and greet her as queen and mother. Ask for protection over your family and home, peace in your household, wisdom about the future, or comfort in grief. Don't expect her to reveal fate outright; listen for quiet knowing. Pour her share, thank her, and keep the yarn as a charm for the home.
invocation:
Frigg of Fensalir, wise and still,
Spinner of fate by silent will,
Queen with the keys of hearth and hall,
Mother who wept at Baldr's fall,
Guard my children, guard my door,
Bless the hearth for evermore.
Weave good fortune strong and fine,
And keep the thread of all that's mine.
Hail Frigg!
offerings: mead, ale, tea or milk
home-baked bread or cakes
spun yarn, knitting, weaving or other handwork
a clean and tidy home
hospitality to a guest or neighbour
flowers from the home garden
beeswax candles
care for children or the elderly
a promise kept to family
avoid: Avoid infidelity and broken household vows in her name. Avoid symbols co-opted by hate groups. Don't press her to reveal fate; she keeps silence for good reason. Keep mistletoe (toxic) away from children and pets.
bestTime: Midwinter, Mother's Night through Yule (Dec–Jan); also any home blessing, wedding or birth.
caution: Norse gods are worshipped today in Heathenry (Ásatrú, Forn Sed and related paths), a living religion with its own customs. Mainstream Heathen organisations reject racism and 'folkish' gatekeeping: no one is barred from the gods by ancestry. Steer clear of symbols and slogans taken up by hate groups (such as the 'Black Sun', the winged Othala rune, or white-power slogans dressed up as Norse lore), and check where your Norse imagery comes from. Mistletoe is poisonous; use it only as a symbol or sealed charm, never ingested.

name: Hel
title: Keeper of the Hall of the Dead
represents: Hel is the ruler of the realm of the dead, also called Hel, which receives those who die of sickness or old age rather than in battle. Shown in the Prose Edda as half living flesh and half dark, she embodies the two faces of death: decay and stillness, rest and the keeping of ancestors. Stern, honest and unbribable, she is the hostess of the quiet dead, the guardian of what's final, and in modern devotion a compassionate keeper of the ancestors.
description:
In Old Norse, hel is first of all a place: the dwelling of the dead, related to words meaning 'to cover' or 'to hide'. As a goddess, Hel appears most fully in Snorri's Prose Edda (13th century). Gylfaginning tells that she is a daughter of Loki and the giantess Angrboða, sister of the wolf Fenrir and the World Serpent. Odin cast her into Niflheim and gave her authority over the nine worlds of the dead, who come to her if they die of sickness or old age. She is half blue-black and half flesh-coloured, grim and stern. Her hall is Éljúðnir, and Snorri gives her household gloomy names: her dish is called Hunger, her knife Famine.

When Baldr died, his brother Hermóðr rode for nine nights on Sleipnir down the Helvegr, across the bridge Gjallarbrú guarded by the maiden Móðguðr, and asked Hel to release him. Hel agreed, but only if every being in the world wept for Baldr. All did except the giantess Þökk (thought to be Loki in disguise), so Baldr stayed. Hel thus appears as just and bound by her word, not simply cruel. Snorri's portrait may be partly literary, shaped by Christian ideas of hell. Older poems treat Hel mainly as a place, and how far she was worshipped as a goddess before the conversion is uncertain.

Today many Heathens and pagans honour Hel as a guardian of the ancestors and of the dead, at Winter Nights, Álfablót and Dísablót, at funerals, and in death-positive and hospice work. Some modern devotees are drawn to her as a patron of endings, chronic illness and hard truths. Her modern 'Hela' image from comics differs greatly from the sources. Norse gods are worshipped today in Heathenry (Ásatrú, Forn Sed and related paths), a living religion with its own customs. Mainstream Heathen organisations reject racism and 'folkish' gatekeeping: no one is barred from the gods by ancestry. Steer clear of symbols and slogans taken up by hate groups (such as the 'Black Sun', the winged Othala rune, or white-power slogans dressed up as Norse lore), and check where your Norse imagery comes from.
items: bones (ethically sourced only) or bone imagery
sacredDays: Winter Nights (Vetrnætr, mid- to late October); Álfablót and ancestor feasts; the dark days of late autumn and winter; funerals and death anniversaries.
howToInvoke: Prepare a quiet, dim space with a black-and-white cloth, a single candle, a bowl of water or mead, and photos or names of your beloved dead. Ground yourself first, feet flat on the floor and breathing slow. Greet her with respect and plain honesty; she doesn't need flattery. Speak the names of your ancestors and ask her to keep them well, to help you accept an ending, to give you courage to face mortality, or to protect you through a dark season. Sit in silence and listen. When finished, thank her, put out the candle, and ground again: eat something, wash your hands, step outside.
invocation:
Hel, Lady of the hidden hall,
Keeper of those who rest from all,
Half in shadow, half in light,
Queen of the long and quiet night,
Hold my dead in gentle keep,
Guard their rest and guard their sleep.
Teach me to honour what must end,
And meet the dark as a faithful friend.
Hail Hel, and peace to those below!
offerings: mead, ale or dark beer (or blackcurrant juice)
a portion of bread and porridge
speaking the names of the dead
candles lit for the ancestors
tending family graves or neglected cemeteries
volunteering in hospice, elder care or chronic-illness support
a poem of mourning or honest remembrance
dark fruits such as blackberries or plums

bestTime: Late autumn into midwinter, Winter Nights to Yule (Oct–Dec), and times of mourning.
caution: Norse gods are worshipped today in Heathenry (Ásatrú, Forn Sed and related paths), a living religion with its own customs. Mainstream Heathen organisations reject racism and 'folkish' gatekeeping: no one is barred from the gods by ancestry. Steer clear of symbols and slogans taken up by hate groups (such as the 'Black Sun', the winged Othala rune, or white-power slogans dressed up as Norse lore), and check where your Norse imagery comes from. Death and ancestor work can stir up grief, so take care of yourself, seek human support, and never use ritual in place of mental-health care. Yew is highly poisonous; handle it only with gloves and keep it away from children and animals.

name: Inanna
title: Queen of Heaven and Earth, the Morning and Evening Star
represents: Inanna is the Sumerian goddess of love, sexual desire and fertility, and equally of war, justice and political power. She is the radiant planet Venus as morning and evening star, the patron goddess of the city of Uruk, and the bold, ambitious Queen of Heaven who claimed the divine powers (me) of civilisation. Her descent into the underworld and return makes her a goddess of death and rebirth, of stripping away and reclaiming, and of facing the shadow.
description:
Inanna was among the most important deities of ancient Mesopotamia, worshipped from the 4th millennium BCE at the Eanna temple in Uruk and later, as Ishtar, throughout Babylonia and Assyria. Her symbols include the reed-bundle gatepost (the cuneiform sign of her name), the eight-pointed star and the rosette. Enheduanna, daughter of King Sargon of Akkad and high priestess at Ur (c. 2300 BCE), composed hymns to her such as 'The Exaltation of Inanna' (Nin-me-šara), among the earliest literature by a named author.

In 'Inanna and Enki' she travels to Eridu, drinks with the god of wisdom, and carries the me, the arts and offices of civilisation, back to Uruk in her boat. Her most famous myth, 'Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld' (known from Old Babylonian tablets), tells how she descended to the realm of her sister Ereshkigal. At each of seven gates she had to give up one of her royal garments and ornaments (crown, lapis beads, breast-jewels, pectoral, gold ring, lapis measuring rod and line, and royal robe) until she stood naked before the underworld judges, who struck her dead and hung her corpse on a hook. After three days and nights her faithful minister Ninshubur won help from Enki, who made two small beings to revive her with the food and water of life. To return she had to give a substitute, and she chose her husband Dumuzi, who hadn't mourned her; his sister Geshtinanna then agreed to share his time below, half a year each.

Ishtar's later Akkadian Descent, the Epic of Gilgamesh (in which she courts Gilgamesh) and the Babylonian festivals of Tammuz and Ishtar continued her cult into the 1st millennium BCE. In modern times, Diane Wolkstein and Samuel Noah Kramer's 'Inanna, Queen of Heaven and Earth' (1983) and Sylvia Brinton Perera's 'Descent to the Goddess' made her a central figure in feminist spirituality and Jungian shadow work. Mesopotamian polytheist revivalists also honour her with reconstructed hymns and offerings. Her ancient cult involved temple personnel and rites, such as the 'sacred marriage', which are still debated by scholars, so be cautious with popular claims.
items: seven veils or garments for descent ritual
sacredDays: The appearance of Venus as morning or evening star; the month of Dumuzi/Tammuz (midsummer, June–July) for mourning and rebirth; New Year (Akitu, spring equinox) in Babylonian tradition; Friday in modern Venusian practice.
howToInvoke: Look for Venus in the dawn or dusk sky and invoke her when the star is visible. Set an altar with lapis lazuli, a gold or red candle, a lamp or star image, dates and a cup of beer or wine. Burn cedar or juniper. Stand with confidence and raise your hand to the star; she is a queen, so speak with both reverence and boldness. For descent and shadow work, take off seven pieces of jewellery or clothing one by one, naming at each 'gate' something you're willing to release, then put them back on as you 'ascend', reclaiming your power. Ask for courage, love, sovereignty, justice or renewal. Thank her and pour the libation outside.
invocation:
Inanna, Lady of the Morning Star,
Queen of Heaven, bright and far,
You who passed the seven gates,
Who faced your sister and your fates,
Stripped of crown and robe and ring,
Yet rose again, the shining Queen,
Lend me courage to descend,
And rise again when trials end.
Lady of love and lady of war,
Shine in me, O Holy Star.
offerings: beer or date wine (or date syrup in water)
dates, figs and apples
butter, cream or sweet cakes
cedar or juniper incense
lapis lazuli beads
a hymn or love poem recited aloud (Enheduanna's tradition)
a lamp or candle lit at the rising of Venus
a bold creative act or advocacy for women's rights in her name
perfume or fine oil
avoid: Don't approach her as a passive or merely decorative 'love goddess'; she is a queen of war and justice too. Avoid treating sacred-prostitution claims as established fact. Respect her as rooted in the history of Iraq and Syria, and honour the living peoples of the region.
bestTime: Whenever Venus is visible as morning or evening star; midsummer (June–July) for the descent and return; spring equinox for new beginnings.
caution: Inanna's descent is powerful shadow-work material and can stir up deep emotion, so be gentle with yourself and seek support if needed. Popular books blend ancient text with modern interpretation; read translations (e.g. the ETCSL corpus) where you can.
